parsed.wine_summary:
One Point Five takes its name from the 1.5 miles between Shafer's winery and their Stags Leap District vineyards — a detail that signals how site-specific this wine is despite carrying the broader Napa Valley AVA designation. Shafer has been farming these eastern hillside and benchland parcels since 1972, and the estate's track record with Cabernet Sauvignon is among the most consistent in the valley. Doug Shafer and winemaker Elias Fernandez built a house style around density and concentration without abandoning structure, and One Point Five sits as the accessible entry point to that philosophy — accessible being relative when you're north of $125.

The wine draws from multiple estate blocks planted on the rocky, well-drained soils characteristic of the Stags Leap palisades. These eastern-facing slopes get morning sun and afternoon shade from the Vaca Mountains, which moderates ripening just enough to preserve acidity at high sugar levels. The result is a Cabernet that tastes ripe and generous but doesn't flatten out on the palate the way some Napa wines at this alcohol level can.
parsed.terroir_expression: Shafer's vineyards sit on the western edge of the Vaca Range, where ancient volcanic activity deposited layers of rocky,ite-rich soil over a base of fractured sedimentary rock from the Franciscan Complex. The benchland soils here are shallow and stony — a mix of volcanic rubble and alluvial gravel washed down from the palisades — which restricts vine vigor and concentrates berry size. The Stags Leap corridor funnels cool afternoon air from San Pablo Bay directly up through the district, dropping temperatures significantly after midday and slowing sugar accumulation relative to the warmer northern valley. In the glass, this translates to dark, concentrated fruit with a graphite-like minerality and enough natural acidity to give the wine tension, even at 15.3% ABV. The rocky soils also contribute to the fine-grained tannin texture that distinguishes Stags Leap Cabernets from the broader, softer profiles you find on the Rutherford benchland.
parsed.vinification_summary: Shafer ferments One Point Five in stainless steel tanks with extended maceration — typically 14 to 18 days of skin contact after primary fermentation completes — to extract deep color and tannin without pulling harsh seed tannins. The wine then goes into French oak barrels, with a significant proportion of new wood (historically around 50-60%), for roughly 20 months. That new oak percentage is high enough to leave a cedar and vanilla imprint, especially in youth, but Shafer's fruit intensity tends to absorb it within a few years. Malolactic fermentation (the conversion of sharp malic acid to softer lactic acid) happens in barrel, which rounds the mid-palate and integrates the oak flavors more seamlessly. The 100% Cabernet Sauvignon composition — no Merlot or Petit Verdot for softening — means structure is entirely dependent on fruit quality and extraction choices.

Lamb shoulder with black olive tapenade and roasted root vegetables — the olive brininess pulls out the wine's savory undertones. Aged Comté or Gruyère on a cheese board — the nutty, caramelized flavors in the cheese echo the wine's oak-derived vanilla and toast without competing with its fruit.
